items.stem: Babur's remarks about Hindustan's "masses of gold and silver" and "unnumbered and endless workmen" help explain which of the following about how Mughal rulers sustained their state?

options.text: They funded the state by taxing a large and productive population of farmers and artisans.
options.why: Babur values India for its wealth and huge labor force. Mughal rulers, especially from Akbar onward, paid for their state and army mainly with land revenue and taxes on a dense agrarian and artisan population, collected through officials and zamindars.
options.label: key

options.text: They paid their armies mainly with plunder seized from Central Asian cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara.
options.why: This turns the situation around. Babur had lost his Central Asian lands to the Uzbeks, and India's wealth, not Central Asian loot, paid for Mughal power.
options.label: reversal

options.text: They depended chiefly on customs payments collected from European trading companies that controlled the major Indian ports.
options.why: European companies did not control major Indian ports or provinces until the mid-eighteenth century and after, long after the Mughal revenue system took shape.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: They drew most of their revenue from silver mines that the state operated directly across northern India.
options.why: Babur says nothing about mines. Northern India had little silver mining, and much of its silver came in through trade, so the Mughal fisc rested on land revenue, not state mines.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "They funded the state by taxing a large and productive population of farmers and artisans.". Babur values India for its wealth and huge labor force. Mughal rulers, especially from Akbar onward, paid for their state and army mainly with land revenue and taxes on a dense agrarian and artisan population, collected through officials and zamindars.
"They paid their armies mainly with plunder seized from Central Asian cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara." is incorrect: This turns the situation around. Babur had lost his Central Asian lands to the Uzbeks, and India's wealth, not Central Asian loot, paid for Mughal power.
"They depended chiefly on customs payments collected from European trading companies that controlled the major Indian ports." is incorrect: European companies did not control major Indian ports or provinces until the mid-eighteenth century and after, long after the Mughal revenue system took shape.
"They drew most of their revenue from silver mines that the state operated directly across northern India." is incorrect: Babur says nothing about mines. Northern India had little silver mining, and much of its silver came in through trade, so the Mughal fisc rested on land revenue, not state mines.
facts: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, at Panipat in 1526.
Under Akbar (r. 1556-1605), the Mughal state paid for itself mainly through land revenue taken from the agrarian population, collected with the help of zamindars and officials.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Babur picks out India's gold and silver and its countless workmen as its main advantages, which points to the population and wealth that Mughal taxation relied on.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly challenge Babur's claim that Indian handicraft had no "form or symmetry, method or quality"?

options.text: Babur's army won at Panipat partly because it used matchlock firearms and field cannon.

options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.why: This is true, but it concerns Portuguese naval power on the coast, not the quality of goods made by Indian artisans.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.why: Indian cotton cloth was one of the most sought-after manufactured goods in Afro-Eurasian trade, and that demand undercuts Babur's dismissal of Indian craftsmanship.
options.label: key

options.text: Merchants shipped large amounts of pepper from the Malabar coast to ports in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf.
options.why: Pepper was a major Indian export, but it is a crop, not a handicraft, so it does not speak to Babur's claim about the quality of Indian work.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

items.stem: Babur's conquest of northern India after the Battle of Panipat, described in the context line, is best understood as part of which broader development?

options.text: European trading companies seized territory in South Asia and ruled through local princes
options.why: European territorial rule in India began in the mid-eighteenth century, after Mughal power had declined, and it was not the setting for Babur's conquest.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Anticolonial movements mobilized peasants and elites to expel foreign conquerors from their lands
options.why: Anticolonial nationalism belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Babur was a conqueror, not someone resisting foreign rule.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Mongol khanates united Eurasian trade routes under the heirs of Chinggis Khan
options.why: Babur claimed descent from Chinggis Khan, but the Mongol khanates that unified Eurasian routes belonged to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, not the 1520s.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Land-based empires used gunpowder weapons to expand and centralize their rule
options.why: Babur used firearms and artillery at Panipat in 1526. Like the Ottomans and Safavids in the same era, the Mughals relied on gunpowder weapons to build and hold a large land empire.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Land-based empires used gunpowder weapons to expand and centralize their rule". Babur used firearms and artillery at Panipat in 1526. Like the Ottomans and Safavids in the same era, the Mughals relied on gunpowder weapons to build and hold a large land empire.

"Anticolonial movements mobilized peasants and elites to expel foreign conquerors from their lands" is incorrect: Anticolonial nationalism belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Babur was a conqueror, not someone resisting foreign rule.
"Mongol khanates united Eurasian trade routes under the heirs of Chinggis Khan" is incorrect: Babur claimed descent from Chinggis Khan, but the Mongol khanates that unified Eurasian routes belonged to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, not the 1520s.
facts: Babur used firearms and field artillery in defeating Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.
In the same era the Ottoman and Safavid empires also used gunpowder weapons to expand, as at the Ottoman victory over the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Babur defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526 and began Mughal rule, which places the source within the expansion of the gunpowder land empires.

"These discussions took place every Thursday night in the Ibadat-Khana, a building at Fatehpur-Sikri, erected for the purpose. For a time Abulfazl took but a subordinate part in the discussions, simply spurring the various Muhammadan sectaries to reply to and demolish each other's arguments. The bigotry, the narrowness, evinced by the leaders of these sectaries, who agreeing that it was right to persecute Hindus and other unbelievers, hurled charges of infidelity against each other, quite disgusted Akbar. He was further disgusted with the rudeness towards each other displayed by the several sectaries, some of them holding high office in the State, and he was compelled on one occasion to warn them that any one of them who should so offend in the future would have to quit the hall."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Malleson makes about the Thursday discussions at Fatehpur-Sikri?

options.text: Akbar banned all Muslim officials from state office after they showed rudeness in the Ibadat-Khana debates

options.why: Malleson says the scholars' bigotry and charges of infidelity against each other quite disgusted Akbar, who found many divisions instead of unity.
options.label: key

options.why: Akbar opened the Ibadat-Khana debates to scholars of other faiths, including Jesuits from Goa in 1580. This shows him seeking answers beyond the quarreling Muslim scholars.

items.stem: Akbar's dissatisfaction with the attitudes described in the excerpt is most consistent with which of his policies toward non-Muslim subjects?

options.text: Organizing non-Muslims into self-governing millets led by their own religious authorities
options.why: The millet system belonged to the Ottoman Empire, not the Mughal Empire.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Ending the jizya and recruiting Hindu Rajput nobles into imperial service

items.stem: The depopulation of Caribbean islands described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the sixteenth-century Caribbean?

options.text: The abolition of the encomienda system across all of Spanish America by royal decree in 1542
options.why: The New Laws of 1542 limited encomiendas, for example by restricting inheritance, but did not abolish them, and colonists resisted them.

Context: Albert Lybyer was an American historian who wrote this study of the Ottoman government in the time of Sultan Suleiman, who ruled from 1520 to 1566.

"The principle of the personality of law and religion came most visibly into play in the heart of the empire. Prevalent in the Orient from the time of Assyria’s greatness to the present day, it is not easily to be understood in a land that has wholly separated religion and law. Where these two ideas are united, two men who hold different faiths must perforce live under different laws. The Ottomans adopted the idea unreservedly and worked it out into a complicated system: each considerable body of their non-Moslem subjects, Greek Orthodox, United Greek, Armenian, and Jewish, they left, in time, not merely to its own religion, but to its own law and the administration of its law in all matters that did not concern Moslems. [...] Proceeding yet farther with the same principle, they granted even greater privileges to foreigners who wished to reside within the empire. Except for a tax upon the land which they might occupy, for the necessity of paying customs duties, and for responsibility to Ottoman courts of justice in civil cases in which Ottoman subjects were concerned, such foreigners were almost wholly free from Ottoman control, freer far to do as they pleased than they could be in their native lands."

"1. Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be founded only upon the general good. 2. The aim of all political association is the preservation of the natural and imprescriptible rights of man. These rights are liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression. 3. Liberty consists in the freedom to do everything which injures no one else; hence the exercise of the natural rights of each man has no limits except those which assure to the other members of the society the enjoyment of the same rights. These limits can only be determined by law. 5. Law can only prohibit such actions as are hurtful to society. Nothing may be prevented which is not forbidden by law, and no one may be forced to do anything not provided for by law. 6. Law is the expression of the general will. Every citizen has a right to participate personally, or through his representative, in its foundation. It must be the same for all, whether it protects or punishes."

"The partition of British India into separate states of India and Pakistan in 1947 amid communal violence" is incorrect: Partition did happen, but it grew out of Hindu-Muslim political division, not out of the excerpt's argument about cooperation.
"The expansion of state-led heavy industry through national five-year economic plans" is incorrect: Nehru's five-year plans started in 1951, after independence, and they were not a strategy for ending British rule.
"The Indian National Army's armed campaign alongside Japanese forces to drive the British out" is incorrect: Subhas Chandra Bose's INA used armed force with Axis support. This was the opposite of the excerpt's focus on withdrawing Indian cooperation.
facts: Gandhi led the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922), which included boycotts of British goods, courts and schools.
Nehru's government launched India's first five-year plan in 1951.
Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army with Japanese support during the Second World War.

items.stem: The five-year plans that the excerpt credits to Jawaharlal Nehru are best explained as an example of which economic approach?

options.text: A mixed economy in which the state directed investment and owned key industries

options.why: Nehru borrowed the idea of planning from the Soviets, but India never forced all farmland into collectives. Indian agriculture stayed mostly in private hands.

options.why: This describes India's reforms that began in 1991, decades after Nehru, and it is the opposite of his state-led planning.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "A mixed economy in which the state directed investment and owned key industries". This fits the excerpt's goals of strong growth and higher incomes for the poor.
"Forced collectivization of all farmland into state farms following the Soviet model under Stalin" is incorrect: Nehru borrowed the idea of planning from the Soviets, but India never forced all farmland into collectives. Indian agriculture stayed mostly in private hands.
"Export-led growth built on low-wage manufacturing for American and European consumers" is incorrect: This was the strategy of East Asian economies such as South Korea and Taiwan. Nehru's India stressed self-reliance and import substitution instead.
"Free-market liberalization that cut tariffs, sold state firms, and invited foreign multinational investment" is incorrect: This describes India's reforms that began in 1991, decades after Nehru, and it is the opposite of his state-led planning.
facts: India's First Five-Year Plan began in 1951 under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
Nehru's India combined state-owned heavy industry with a private sector, an arrangement usually called a mixed economy.

items.stem: The refugee movement across the new India-Pakistan borders described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader process?

options.text: Cold War proxy conflicts in which the United States and Soviet Union armed rival Indian states
options.why: Partition came from the end of British rule and from communal divisions, not from superpower proxy wars between Indian states.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Rural-to-urban migration caused by Green Revolution mechanization of farming in Punjab
options.why: The Green Revolution began in the mid-1960s, long after the refugee movements of 1947.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Post-1945 decolonization that drew new borders along religious or ethnic lines

options.label: key

options.text: Late nineteenth-century migration of indentured South Asian laborers to plantations in the Caribbean and Africa
options.why: Indentured labor migration was a feature of nineteenth-century imperialism, not of the 1947 independence settlement.

The correct answer is "Post-1945 decolonization that drew new borders along religious or ethnic lines". Britain withdrew from South Asia in 1947 and partitioned it largely along Hindu-Muslim lines. "Cold War proxy conflicts in which the United States and Soviet Union armed rival Indian states" is incorrect: Partition came from the end of British rule and from communal divisions, not from superpower proxy wars between Indian states.
"Rural-to-urban migration caused by Green Revolution mechanization of farming in Punjab" is incorrect: The Green Revolution began in the mid-1960s, long after the refugee movements of 1947.
"Late nineteenth-century migration of indentured South Asian laborers to plantations in the Caribbean and Africa" is incorrect: Indentured labor migration was a feature of nineteenth-century imperialism, not of the 1947 independence settlement.
facts: Britain partitioned British India into India and Pakistan at independence in 1947.

items.stem: The context line says this study was written for the U.S. government in 1995. Which situation in India at that time best explains U.S. interest in India's economic history?

options.text: India had begun liberalizing its economy in 1991, raising U.S. interest in trade
options.why: The 1991 reforms opened India to foreign trade and investment. This made background on India's economy useful to U.S. officials in the mid-1990s.
options.label: key

options.text: Britain had just granted India independence, so U.S. diplomats needed new information
options.why: Independence came in 1947, nearly fifty years before the study was written.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: India had just founded the Non-Aligned Movement, rejecting alliance with either superpower
options.why: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961, and the Cold War had ended by 1995.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: India had recently adopted Soviet-style central planning for the first time under Indira Gandhi
options.why: Planning began under Nehru in 1951, as the excerpt notes. By 1995 India was moving away from planning, not taking it up.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "India had begun liberalizing its economy in 1991, raising U.S. interest in trade". The 1991 reforms opened India to foreign trade and investment. This made background on India's economy useful to U.S. officials in the mid-1990s.
"Britain had just granted India independence, so U.S. diplomats needed new information" is incorrect: Independence came in 1947, nearly fifty years before the study was written.
"India had just founded the Non-Aligned Movement, rejecting alliance with either superpower" is incorrect: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961, and the Cold War had ended by 1995.
"India had recently adopted Soviet-style central planning for the first time under Indira Gandhi" is incorrect: Planning began under Nehru in 1951, as the excerpt notes. By 1995 India was moving away from planning, not taking it up.
facts: India began major economic liberalization reforms in 1991.
The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961.
